(CNN) -- The Czech Republic's practice of surgically castrating convicted sex offenders is "invasive, irreversible and mutilating" and should stop immediately, the Council of Europe's Anti-Torture Committee said in a report made public Thursday. The central European country castrated at least 94 prisoners in the 10 years up to April 2008, when investigators from the Council of Europe, a human-rights forum, visited the Czech Republic. The Council of Europe condemned the practice as "degrading." The procedure is being performed even on first-time, non-violent offenders, such as exhibitionists, its investigation revealed. Prisoners have to request castration under Czech law, but many fear they will be jailed for life if they do not, the investigation found. "In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention," the report said. "Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention." And it warned that some "significantly" mentally retarded people had been castrated. "In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated," the report said. "In all of these instances, the court-appointed guardian had signed the consent form; in two cases, the guardians were mayors." The investigators found only two convicts who had spontaneously volunteered for castration, while others they interviewed said mental health staff specializing in sexuality had recommended it. "The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient's admission to hospital," the report said. "Some of the sexologists interviewed by the delegation themselves affirmed that for certain patients there was no alternative treatment to surgical castration." The Czech Republic defends the practice as voluntary, saying castration aims permanently to reduce testosterone levels in order to diminish the offender's sexual urges. The process, officially called "therapeutic testicular pulpectomies ... are performed upon a written request of an adult man," the Czech government responded. It said the operation had to be approved by a committee of experts. "Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive," the Czech government said, saying the Council of Europe had not proven its case sufficiently for the country to abandon castration. It argues the procedure is effective in reducing repeat offenses. But the Council of Europe questioned the statistics on repeat offenses and said even if they were correct, castration was not an appropriate way to reduce recidivism. "The committee's delegation came across three cases in which sex offenders had committed serious sex-related crimes, including serial rape and attempted murder, after they had been surgically castrated," the human-rights group said. "Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders," the report said. It said candidates for castration often received information about the procedure which was too technical to understand -- or no information at all. "Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed," the report warned. It condemned the practice as "an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis," also warning of possible depression and changes in appearance. It said it was impossible to determine how many people had been castrated in keeping with a 1966 law. The Council of Europe delegation visited the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008. It issued its report and the Czech response on July 23, 2008. It made them public on Thursday at the request of the Czech government, it said.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — The Czech Republic’s practice of surgically castrating convicted sex offenders is “invasive, irreversible and mutilating” and should be halted immediately, the Council of Europe’s Anti-Torture Committee said in a report made public Thursday.

The Central European country castrated at least 94 prisoners during the 10 years preceding April 2008, when investigators from the Council of Europe, a human-rights forum, visited the Czech Republic.

The Council of Europe condemned the practice as “degrading.” Its investigation found that the procedure was performed even on first-time, nonviolent offenders, including exhibitionists.

Under Czech law, prisoners must request castration. However, the investigation found that many feared they would be imprisoned for life if they did not.

“In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention,” the report said. “Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention.”

The report also warned that some people with “significant” mental disabilities had been castrated.

“In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated,” the report said. “In all of these instances, the court-appointed guardian had signed the consent form; in two cases, the guardians were mayors.”

Investigators found only two convicts who had volunteered for castration without prompting. Others interviewed said that mental health professionals specializing in sexuality had recommended the procedure.

“The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient’s admission to hospital,” the report said. “Some of the sexologists interviewed by the delegation themselves affirmed that for certain patients there was no alternative treatment to surgical castration.”

The Czech Republic has defended the practice as voluntary, saying that castration is intended to permanently reduce testosterone levels and thereby diminish an offender’s sexual urges.

The procedure, officially described as “therapeutic testicular pulpectomies,” is “performed upon a written request of an adult man,” the Czech government said in its response. It added that the operation must be approved by a committee of experts.

“Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive,” the Czech government said. It maintained that the Council of Europe had not sufficiently proven its case to justify abandoning the practice.

The government also argued that the procedure is effective in reducing repeat offenses.

The Council of Europe, however, questioned the recidivism statistics and said that, even if they were accurate, castration was not an appropriate means of reducing repeat offenses.

“The committee’s delegation came across three cases in which sex offenders had committed serious sex-related crimes, including serial rape and attempted murder, after they had been surgically castrated,” the human-rights group said.

“Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders,” the report said.

The report also found that candidates for castration often received information about the procedure that was either too technical to understand or entirely absent.

“Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed,” the report warned.

It condemned the practice as “an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis.” The report also warned of possible depression and changes in appearance.

The Council of Europe said it was impossible to determine how many people had been castrated under a 1966 law.

Its delegation visited the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008. The Council issued its report, along with the Czech government’s response, on July 23, 2008, and made both documents public Thursday at the Czech government’s request.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — The Council of Europe’s Anti-Torture Committee has called on the Czech Republic to end the surgical castration of convicted sex offenders without delay, describing the operation as physically damaging, permanent, and highly intrusive.

According to a report released publicly on Thursday, at least 94 inmates underwent castration during the decade preceding April 2008. Investigators from the Council of Europe, a human-rights organization, visited the Central European nation between March 25 and April 2 of that year. The organization characterized the policy as degrading.

The inquiry found that the surgery was not limited to violent or repeat offenders. Some nonviolent individuals with no previous convictions, including exhibitionists, were also subjected to the procedure.

Although Czech law requires prisoners to apply for castration themselves, investigators questioned whether such consent was truly voluntary. Many patients said their decision had been influenced, at least in part, by concern that refusing the operation could result in indefinite or lifelong confinement. Some reported that their treating sexologists had directly presented surgery as their only route out of permanent detention.

The committee also raised concerns about the castration of individuals with significant intellectual disabilities. It identified at least five legally incapacitated offenders who had undergone the procedure. In each case, a guardian appointed by the court signed the consent document; in two of those instances, the guardian was a mayor.

Only two convicted offenders encountered by investigators appeared to have volunteered for castration entirely on their own initiative. Other patients said specialists in sexual mental health had proposed the operation, sometimes less than a week after the patient entered a hospital. Several sexologists interviewed by the delegation likewise said they believed surgery was the only possible treatment for certain patients.

Czech authorities maintain that the procedure is voluntary and is intended to produce a lasting reduction in testosterone, thereby weakening offenders’ sexual impulses. In its formal response, the government referred to the operation as a “therapeutic testicular pulpectomy” and said it could be carried out only after an adult man submitted a written request.

Officials added that an expert panel must authorize the surgery and that the patient must consent before it takes place. The government said castration is considered for sexually aggressive men who are unable to control their sexual drives. It argued that the Council of Europe had not presented enough evidence to justify ending the practice.

The Czech government also contends that castration lowers the likelihood of further offenses. The Council of Europe challenged the reliability of the recidivism figures, however, and said that even accurate statistics would not make surgery an acceptable method of preventing repeat crimes.

During its visit, the delegation identified three surgically castrated offenders who later committed serious sexual crimes, among them serial rape and attempted murder. The committee further stated that surgical castration is no longer broadly recognized by the medical community as an accepted treatment for sex offenders.

Investigators also found shortcomings in the information given to prospective patients. In some cases, explanations were so technical that patients could not understand them; in others, no information was provided. Several men who had already undergone the surgery told the delegation they would not have requested it if they had been properly informed beforehand.

The report emphasized that the operation cannot be reversed, invariably causes infertility, and substantially raises the long-term risk of osteoporosis. It also cited possible depression and physical changes in appearance.

The committee said it could not establish the total number of people castrated under legislation dating to 1966. The Council of Europe issued both its findings and the Czech government’s response on July 23, 2008. It later made the documents public on Thursday at the Czech government’s request.

The Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment investigated the Czech Republic’s use of surgical castration as a treatment for convicted sex offenders. During its inquiry, the committee examined medical and judicial records and interviewed prisoners, psychiatric patients, doctors, and other staff involved in the treatment and supervision of offenders.

The investigation found that at least 94 sex offenders had undergone surgical castration. The operation, which involves the irreversible removal of hormone-producing tissue from the testicles, was not limited to violent repeat offenders considered to present an exceptional danger. Those operated on reportedly included first-time offenders, people convicted of nonviolent crimes, men with intellectual or mental disabilities, and individuals who had been declared legally incapable of making decisions for themselves.

Czech authorities maintained that the procedure was performed only with the patient’s consent and after other treatment options had been considered. The committee, however, questioned whether consent given in prison or compulsory psychiatric detention could ever be regarded as fully free. Some offenders appeared to believe that castration would improve their chances of release, reduce the length of their confinement, or allow them to avoid indefinite detention or continued treatment. In those circumstances, the committee concluded that patients could be subjected to intense pressure even when no explicit threat was made.

The committee also raised concerns about the quality of the consent process, particularly in cases involving mentally disabled or legally incapacitated people. Because surgical castration is permanent and can have serious physical and psychological consequences, it said that formal approval by a patient, guardian, or medical panel was not enough to eliminate the risk of coercion or abuse.

In its assessment, the committee emphasized that less invasive and reversible methods were available, including psychotherapy, medication, and hormonal treatment, together with structured risk-management programs. It rejected the argument that surgical castration was necessary to protect the public or prevent reoffending.

The committee ultimately described the practice as a degrading form of treatment and called on the Czech authorities to end it immediately. It urged the country to replace surgical castration with modern, evidence-based therapies that respect patients’ dignity, bodily integrity, and right to give genuinely free and informed consent.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about the Council of Europe condemning the Czech Republic’s surgical castration of convicted sex offenders.
counterfactuals.output:
**Council of Europe condemns Czech surgical castration of sex offenders**

**PRAGUE, Czech Republic** — The Council of Europe’s anti-torture watchdog has condemned the Czech Republic’s use of surgical castration on convicted sex offenders, calling the irreversible procedure degrading and urging authorities to end it immediately.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture said removing offenders’ testicles could not be justified as a treatment for sexual violence, even when patients had formally consented. It questioned whether consent could be genuinely voluntary when offenders may view surgery as a way to secure release from detention or psychiatric treatment.

Czech authorities have defended the practice as a rare, voluntary option offered only after medical and psychological assessment. Supporters say it can sharply reduce sexual drive and the risk of repeat offenses in individuals considered particularly dangerous.

The committee rejected those arguments, saying surgical castration causes permanent physical changes and carries serious psychological and ethical consequences. It said less invasive treatments, including medication and psychotherapy, should be used instead.

The dispute has highlighted broader divisions over how European countries manage high-risk sex offenders after conviction. Chemical castration, which uses medication to suppress testosterone and is generally reversible, is permitted in several countries under varying legal safeguards. Surgical castration is far less common.

The Council of Europe, a 46-member human rights organization separate from the European Union, cannot directly force the Czech Republic to change its laws. Its findings, however, can increase political and legal pressure on governments accused of violating European standards on humane treatment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the findings of the Council of Europe Anti-Torture Committee’s 2008 investigation into surgical castration practices in the Czech Republic, including the Czech government’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
The Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), following its March–April 2008 visit to the Czech Republic, examined the use of surgical castration—irreversible removal of the testes—as a treatment for detained sex offenders.

### CPT findings

- Surgical castration was not confined to exceptionally rare cases; dozens of offenders had undergone the procedure, including prisoners and patients held under court-ordered “protective treatment.”
- The CPT doubted that consent could be genuinely free when patients faced the prospect of prolonged or potentially indefinite confinement and believed castration might improve their chances of release.
- In some cases, records did not demonstrate that less invasive treatments—psychotherapy, medication or reversible hormonal treatment—had first been adequately tried.
- The committee also questioned whether patients were always fully informed about irreversible physical and psychological consequences, including infertility, hormonal changes, osteoporosis and other long-term effects.
- It found the legal and procedural safeguards insufficient, particularly regarding independent assessment, informed consent and the connection between castration and decisions on discharge.
- The CPT concluded that surgical castration was a mutilating, irreversible intervention that could not be considered medically necessary in this context and could amount to degrading treatment. It called on the Czech authorities to stop using it immediately and to rely on reversible treatment and risk-management measures instead.

### Czech government’s response

The Czech government rejected the CPT’s demand for abolition. It maintained that:

- castration was performed only at the patient’s written request;
- requests were reviewed by specialist doctors and an expert commission;
- patients were informed of the consequences and could withdraw consent;
- the operation was reserved for severe cases in which other treatments had failed or were unsuitable;
- castration was not formally a legal condition for release, which remained a matter for the courts; and
- Czech clinical experience showed a very low rate of sexual reoffending among castrated patients.

The government accepted that rules and consent procedures could be clarified or strengthened and referred to planned legislative safeguards, but it continued to regard surgical castration as a lawful, effective last-resort treatment. Thus, the central disagreement remained: the CPT viewed consent in a custodial setting as inherently compromised and the procedure as unacceptable, while the Czech authorities characterized it as voluntary medical treatment subject to professional oversight.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article explaining why human-rights investigators called the Czech practice of castrating sex offenders invasive, irreversible, mutilating, and degrading.
counterfactuals.output:
# Investigators Condemn Czech Surgical Castration of Sex Offenders as Degrading Treatment

**PRAGUE —** European human-rights investigators sharply criticized the Czech Republic’s use of surgical castration on convicted sex offenders, describing the procedure as an “invasive, irreversible and mutilating intervention” that could amount to degrading treatment, particularly when performed on men held in prisons or secure psychiatric institutions.

The criticism came from the Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture, or CPT, following inspections of Czech detention and psychiatric facilities in the late 2000s. Investigators found that surgical castration had been used as part of the country’s system for treating sex offenders and managing the risk of reoffending.

Czech officials defended the procedure as voluntary, medically supervised and effective in carefully selected cases. But the committee concluded that the circumstances in which consent was obtained made it difficult to regard the choice as genuinely free.

## A permanent physical intervention

Surgical castration involves removing or disabling testicular tissue, causing a substantial and permanent reduction in testosterone production. Unlike anti-androgen drugs—sometimes called chemical castration—which can generally be stopped, the surgical procedure cannot be reversed.

The consequences can include infertility, loss of sexual function, hot flashes, fatigue, changes in body composition, reduced bone density and psychological distress. Testosterone replacement may address some effects, but doing so can undermine the procedure’s intended suppression of sexual drive.

For investigators, that permanence was central to the ethical problem. The operation does not merely manage symptoms temporarily; it permanently alters a person’s body and reproductive capacity. The CPT therefore characterized it as invasive, irreversible and mutilating.

The term “mutilating” reflected the removal or destruction of healthy sexual organs for behavioral-control purposes, rather than treatment of a disease affecting those organs. Human-rights experts also questioned whether such an operation could be justified when less intrusive treatments—including psychotherapy, psychiatric care, supervision and medication—were available.

## Consent under pressure

The most serious concern was whether detained offenders could provide valid consent.

Under the Czech system examined by the committee, some sex offenders were subject to court-ordered treatment in secure psychiatric facilities. Their discharge could depend on medical assessments of whether they remained dangerous. Investigators said patients could therefore believe that accepting surgery would improve their chances of release, while refusing it might mean remaining confined for an indefinite period.

That created what the committee viewed as an inherently coercive setting.

Even if a patient signed a consent form, investigators said the decision might not be truly voluntary when the alternatives appeared to be continued detention, a less favorable risk assessment or uncertainty about eventual release. In human-rights and medical ethics, consent must be informed and given without improper pressure. Formal agreement alone is not enough.

The CPT also raised questions about whether all patients had received clear information on the procedure’s permanent consequences, possible complications and available alternatives. The vulnerability of people held in psychiatric institutions—including some with mental-health or intellectual impairments—made robust safeguards especially important.

## Doubts about medical necessity

Czech authorities argued that castration could sharply reduce sexual drive and lower the risk of repeat offending. They said the operation was reserved for a small group of men, performed only after expert review and chosen by patients who had not benefited sufficiently from other treatment.

Investigators did not dismiss the state’s obligation to protect the public from serious sexual violence. But they said public safety could not automatically justify an irreversible operation, especially when performed on detained people whose ability to refuse was compromised.

The committee also questioned whether the claimed benefits had been established strongly enough to outweigh the physical and ethical costs. Low reoffending rates among castrated offenders, it noted, did not by themselves prove that surgery was responsible. Patients selected for the operation might also receive intensive therapy, medication, supervision and other forms of treatment.

Modern human-rights standards generally require clinicians to use the least restrictive and least invasive intervention capable of achieving a legitimate therapeutic goal. In the committee’s view, permanent surgery failed that test when reversible options remained available.

## Why investigators called it degrading

The European Convention on Human Rights prohibits torture and “inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.” The CPT’s mandate is preventive: it inspects places where people are deprived of liberty and identifies practices that may violate that prohibition.

A medical procedure does not escape scrutiny simply because doctors perform it or because it is described as treatment. Investigators examine its purpose, necessity, proportionality, physical effects and the circumstances in which consent is obtained.

Several factors led the committee to describe Czech surgical castration as degrading:

- It permanently altered intimate and reproductive organs.
- It carried significant lifelong physical and psychological consequences.
- It was used on people under state control.
- Refusal could appear to reduce the prospect of release from secure treatment.
- Less invasive and potentially reversible alternatives existed.
- Questions remained about whether consent was fully informed and free of pressure.

The procedure could therefore diminish a patient’s dignity and bodily autonomy, investigators said, even when it was not intended as punishment.

## Czech defense and demands for reform

Czech officials maintained that the operation was governed by medical rules and required the patient’s consent. They also cited the need to treat offenders with severe sexual disorders and prevent further victims.

The CPT nevertheless called for the practice to end in the context of detained sex offenders. Human-rights bodies urged the Czech authorities to strengthen independent review, improve access to psychotherapy and reversible medication, and ensure that decisions about release were not tied—explicitly or implicitly—to acceptance of surgery.

The dispute highlighted a broader conflict between public protection and individual rights. States have a duty to manage people who present a serious risk of sexual violence, but they must do so without imposing treatment that is coercive, disproportionate or destructive of bodily integrity.

For the investigators, the decisive issue was not sympathy for offenders or denial of the harm caused by sexual crimes. It was whether the state could permanently remove or disable healthy sexual organs from people whose liberty—and hopes of release—depended on the same institutions asking them to consent.

Their answer was that, under those conditions, surgical castration crossed the line from treatment into an invasive, irreversible and degrading interference with the human body.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the controversy over “voluntary” surgical castration of Czech sex offenders, covering coerced consent, legally incapacitated patients, recidivism claims, and health risks.
counterfactuals.output:
## Controversy over Czech surgical castration of sex offenders

The Czech Republic has long been one of the few European states to permit **surgical castration—irreversible removal or disabling of the testes—as treatment for some men diagnosed with paraphilic disorders who have committed, or are considered likely to commit, serious sexual offences**. Czech authorities have presented the operation as voluntary and medically indicated. European and international human-rights bodies have challenged both claims.

### Coerced or constrained consent

The central dispute is whether consent can be genuinely voluntary when a patient is confined in a psychiatric hospital, undergoing court-ordered treatment, or hoping that surgery will improve the prospect of release.

The Council of Europe’s **Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT)** found that some patients understood castration as the only realistic route out of potentially indefinite detention. Even without physical force or an explicit legal requirement, the choice could amount to:

- accept irreversible surgery; or  
- remain confined, possibly for an uncertain period.

The CPT therefore argued that formal signatures and repeated requests did not necessarily establish free consent. It characterized surgical castration of detained sex offenders as a **mutilating and irreversible intervention** and said its use in that setting could constitute degrading treatment. Czech officials responded that candidates were informed of alternatives, evaluated by specialists, and free to withdraw their requests.

### Legally incapacitated patients

Investigators also identified cases involving men who had been declared wholly or partly legally incapacitated. Historically, Czech practice could rely on approval from a guardian, court, or expert body in addition to—or in place of legally effective consent from the patient.

Critics argued that substituted authorization is particularly problematic for a non-emergency procedure that:

- permanently destroys fertility;
- substantially alters sexual and hormonal functioning; and
- is undertaken partly for public-safety or criminal-justice purposes.

Human-rights bodies maintained that such an operation should not be performed on a person unable to give full, informed, and legally valid consent. Czech reforms later introduced tighter eligibility and approval rules, but critics continued to question whether any detained or incapacitated patient could make a sufficiently autonomous decision.

### Claims of reduced recidivism

Czech clinicians and officials defended the practice by citing extremely low—and in some presentations zero—sexual reoffending among surgically castrated patients. Those figures were used to portray castration as an unusually effective option for a small group of high-risk offenders for whom psychotherapy or medication had failed.

The evidence has important limitations:

- castrated patients were highly selected rather than randomly assigned;
- studies often involved small samples;
- definitions of reoffending and periods of follow-up varied;
- some offences may not have been reported or detected;
- patients often received psychotherapy, supervision, or institutional care at the same time; and
- advancing age itself reduces average sexual-reoffending risk.

Consequently, the figures do not prove that surgery alone caused the reported reduction. Critics also stress that preventing reoffending cannot by itself justify an irreversible intervention obtained under coercive conditions. Czech specialists counter that, for carefully selected patients with severe paraphilic disorders, reduced testosterone and sexual drive may provide a real therapeutic and preventive benefit.

### Health risks

Surgical castration produces permanent testosterone deficiency unless hormone replacement is provided—replacement that may conflict with the purpose of suppressing sexual drive. Reported or recognized consequences include:

- irreversible infertility;
- major reduction in libido and erectile function;
- hot flushes and fatigue;
- loss of muscle mass and increased body fat;
- osteoporosis and fracture risk;
- metabolic and possible cardiovascular complications;
- anemia and other effects of androgen deficiency;
- depression, emotional changes, and harm to body image; and
- ordinary surgical risks such as bleeding, infection, and complications from anesthesia.

Although medication-based “chemical castration” is usually reversible and adjustable, it also carries significant hormonal and metabolic risks. Critics nevertheless regard it, alongside psychotherapy and structured risk management, as less invasive than removing healthy organs.

### Legal and policy outcome

Following criticism from the CPT, the UN Committee against Torture, and other organizations, Czech law and practice were tightened. Eligibility became more restricted, specialist review was strengthened, and additional safeguards were introduced. The procedure was reserved for exceptional cases involving serious paraphilic disorders, substantial risk, and failure or unsuitability of less invasive measures.

The basic disagreement remains unresolved:

- **Czech defenders** describe surgery as a rare, patient-requested treatment that may permit community life and prevent serious harm.  
- **Opponents** argue that consent obtained under indefinite detention or pressure for release is not truly voluntary, that incapacitated people cannot authorize such an irreversible procedure, that recidivism claims are methodologically weak, and that the operation’s permanent health consequences make it disproportionate.

Thus, the controversy is not only about clinical effectiveness. It concerns whether criminal-justice pressure can ever be separated from medical consent when the offered intervention is irreversible and the alternative may be prolonged loss of liberty.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a CNN news story based on the July 2008 Council of Europe report that found at least 94 Czech prisoners had been surgically castrated during the preceding decade.
counterfactuals.output:
## Report: At least 94 Czech prisoners surgically castrated over decade

**PRAGUE, Czech Republic (CNN)** — At least 94 prisoners in the Czech Republic underwent surgical castration during the decade preceding 2008, according to a Council of Europe report that raised serious concerns about whether inmates could freely consent to the irreversible procedure.

The report, issued by the council’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture following a 2008 review of Czech detention facilities, examined the use of surgical castration as a treatment for men convicted of sexual offenses.

The committee said the operation — which involves removing hormone-producing tissue from the testicles — has permanent physical and psychological consequences. It questioned whether consent given in prison or psychiatric detention could be considered genuinely voluntary, particularly when offenders might believe the procedure would improve their chances of release.

European inspectors also challenged the medical necessity of surgical castration, noting the availability of less invasive and reversible treatments, including medication and psychotherapy.

The committee called on Czech authorities to end the practice in the treatment of detained sex offenders.

Czech officials maintained that the procedure was performed only after a patient requested it and after approval by medical specialists. Authorities have described castration as one part of a broader treatment system intended to reduce the risk that serious sexual offenders will reoffend.

But the Council of Europe said safeguards surrounding consent did not resolve its fundamental objections.

The report intensified debate over how European countries should balance public safety, prisoners’ rights and the treatment of people convicted of sexual crimes. Surgical castration has largely been abandoned elsewhere in Europe, while some countries permit so-called chemical castration, which uses drugs to suppress testosterone and is generally reversible after treatment ends.
